title: Accepting EBT/SNAP: A Retailer Guide
seo_title: Accepting EBT/SNAP: A Retailer Guide | MCCPS
meta_description: A retailer's overview of accepting EBT and SNAP: USDA authorization, eligible items, PIN debit processing, equipment and basic compliance considerations.
dek: What it takes to accept EBT cards, from federal authorization to terminals and day-to-day handling, and what to confirm before you apply.
intro: For many grocery stores, convenience stores and farmers market vendors, accepting EBT is a way to serve a large group of customers who otherwise might shop elsewhere. But EBT is not just another card type you switch on. It involves federal authorization, specific equipment and rules about what can be sold.
This guide gives a general overview. Requirements are set by government agencies and can change, so treat it as a starting point and confirm the details with the program authority before you apply.

paragraphs: EBT stands for electronic benefits transfer, the system that delivers government benefits through a debit-style card. The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, provides food benefits, while some states also load cash benefits onto the same EBT card. Customers use a PIN to pay, much like a debit card.

SNAP and cash benefits are separate balances. SNAP funds can only buy eligible foods. Cash benefits are more flexible, but are subject to state rules about where and how they can be used. A single EBT card may carry both, and your terminal will prompt for which account to use.

Not every store type fits neatly. Convenience stores, small grocers, farmers market vendors, bakeries and specialty food shops have different stocking patterns, and eligibility depends on what you carry. Some vendors at farmers markets use mobile devices or market-run systems for EBT. If you sell at events or markets, ask the market organizer and your processor about the options that apply to you.

To accept SNAP benefits in the United States, a retailer generally must apply to and be authorized by the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food and Nutrition Service. Authorization depends on factors such as the variety and stock of eligible food you carry. Applicants typically submit business information and supporting details, and the agency may verify the store.

Once authorized, you receive an authorization number used when setting up payment processing. Do not start accepting EBT before you are authorized, as unauthorized acceptance can lead to penalties. Rules for cash benefits are set by states, and requirements can differ. Check the current process with the agency and your state.
bullets: Apply for authorization before accepting SNAP benefits
Learn the eligible and ineligible item rules
Confirm state requirements for cash benefits
Ask your processor how to link your authorization to your account

paragraphs: EBT transactions are PIN-based, so you need a terminal with a PIN pad that supports EBT. Some retailers use a countertop terminal, others integrate EBT into their POS. Not every terminal or POS supports it, and some require special certification. Some businesses with manual vouchers or offline fallback options are also subject to rules for those methods.

Processing differs from regular credit cards. EBT is typically a separate transaction type with its own routing, settlement and fees. EBT funds generally do not allow tips or cash back on SNAP balances, and there are rules about voids, refunds and balance inquiries. Ask your provider how EBT appears on your statement, since fees for EBT transactions are often handled differently from credit card fees.

Offline procedures matter. If the network goes down, some retailers have a manual voucher fallback, but those carry specific rules and risks, including that the transaction may not be guaranteed. Ask your provider how outages are handled before you need to know, and make sure your staff are not improvising during an outage.

A typical sale proceeds like this. The cashier totals eligible and ineligible items separately, since SNAP can pay only for eligible foods. The customer swipes or inserts the EBT card, selects the SNAP account, and enters a PIN. The terminal checks the balance and approves up to the available amount. Any remaining balance, including ineligible items, is paid with another method.

Sales tax generally does not apply to SNAP-eligible purchases paid with benefits, but local rules govern the details, so verify your state's treatment. Receipts typically show the remaining balance. Train staff to avoid asking customers to share PINs and to keep the PIN pad private.
steps: Separate SNAP-eligible items from ineligible items at the register.
Customer selects the SNAP or cash benefit account on the PIN pad.
Customer enters the PIN; the terminal checks the balance.
Approve the eligible total, up to the available benefits.
Collect payment for the remainder through another tender.
Provide the receipt showing the remaining balance.

paragraphs: Misuse of EBT, such as accepting benefits for ineligible items or exchanging benefits for cash, is taken seriously and can lead to disqualification or other penalties. Make sure staff know the rules, especially in busy stores with high turnover. Post any required signs and keep your authorization details accessible.

Other pitfalls include inadequate backup procedures when the system is down, improper handling of refunds, and unclear processes for split tender. Write a one-page procedure for your cashiers and review it regularly. Rules change, so confirm requirements with the relevant agency instead of relying on memory.

A practical safeguard is to separate the register screens or buttons for eligible and ineligible items, where your POS allows it. This reduces mistakes when the cashier is busy, and it makes later audits easier. Reviewing a sample of EBT transactions each month is a good habit for owners who are not at the register every day.

sections.h2: Getting set up with your processor
paragraphs: Tell your processor early that you plan to accept EBT, so they can confirm that your terminal or POS supports it and help add it to your account. You will typically provide your authorization information. Ask how fees work, how funds are deposited, and what support is available for EBT questions.

This article is general information; confirm program rules with the USDA and your state agency.

key_takeaways: SNAP acceptance requires authorization from the USDA Food and Nutrition Service.
EBT is PIN-based and needs compatible terminal or POS equipment.
SNAP funds can only buy eligible foods; cash benefits follow state rules.
EBT processing and fees are handled differently from credit cards.
Train staff on eligibility, PIN privacy and prohibited practices.

faq.q: Do I need approval to accept SNAP?
faq.a: Generally yes. Retailers must apply to and be authorized by the USDA Food and Nutrition Service before accepting SNAP benefits. Confirm the current process on the agency's website.

faq.q: Can I use my regular terminal for EBT?
faq.a: Only if it has a PIN pad and supports EBT transactions. Some terminals can be updated or re-programmed. Ask your processor to check your model before buying new equipment.

faq.q: Can customers get cash back on SNAP?
faq.a: SNAP balances cannot be used for cash back. Cash benefit accounts, where offered by the state, have separate rules. Confirm current requirements with your state agency.
SNAP generally covers eligible food items for home preparation and consumption, and not items like alcohol, tobacco or hot prepared foods in most cases. Check the current official eligibility list.

faq.q: Are EBT fees the same as credit card fees?
faq.a: No. EBT is typically processed as a separate PIN-based transaction with its own fee structure. Ask your provider how EBT is priced and how it appears on your statement.
